lessons.title: Evaluating Soil Texture, pH, and Fertility
lessons.body:
Sweet potatoes grow best in loose, well-drained soil. To check texture, grab a handful of moist soil and squeeze it into a ball. If it holds shape but crumbles when you poke it, it's loam â ideal. If it forms a sticky ribbon, it's clay â too heavy. If it won't hold together, it's sand â too loose. For sweet potatoes, you want sandy loam or loam. In Africa, many soils are sandy or clayey; you can improve them with organic matter.

Soil pH affects nutrient availability. Sweet potatoes prefer pH 5.8 to 6.2, but they tolerate 4.5 to 7.5. You can test pH with a simple kit from an agro-dealer (cost about $5â$10) or by sending a sample to a district agricultural office. To raise pH (make less acidic), add wood ash or lime. To lower pH, add elemental sulfur or pine needles. But don't guess â test first.

Fertility: sweet potatoes need moderate nitrogen, high phosphorus, and high potassium. A common recommendation is 200 kg/ha of NPK 6-10-20 or similar. But without a soil test, you might waste money. Look for signs: pale leaves mean nitrogen deficiency; purple leaves mean phosphorus deficiency; yellow edges mean potassium deficiency. Also, add compost or manure â 5 to 10 tons per hectare â to boost organic matter and nutrients.

In Africa, many soils are degraded. Rotate with legumes like beans or groundnuts to fix nitrogen. Avoid fields where sweet potatoes or other root crops grew last season to prevent pest buildup. If you must reuse a field, apply extra compost. Remember, healthy soil = healthy roots. A simple test: dig a hole 30 cm deep; if you see earthworms and dark soil, it's fertile. If hardpan or pale soil, you need amendments.

Finally, check drainage. Sweet potatoes rot in waterlogged soil. Dig a 30 cm hole, fill with water, and see how long it takes to drain. If still there after 2 hours, choose another site or make raised beds. Good texture, correct pH, and adequate fertility set the foundation for a bumper harvest.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Field: Drainage and Slope
lessons.body:
Sweet potatoes hate wet feet. Waterlogged soil causes root rot, especially during heavy rains. Choose a field that slopes gently â 2% to 5% is ideal. This allows excess water to run off without causing erosion. If your land is flat, you can still grow sweet potatoes, but you must make raised beds or ridges. Avoid low-lying areas where water collects after rain. In many parts of Africa, valleys and depressions flood; keep sweet potatoes on higher ground.

Check drainage by digging a 30 cm deep hole and filling it with water. If water drains within 1â2 hours, drainage is good. If it takes 4+ hours, it's poor. For poor drainage, either install drainage ditches (30 cm deep around the field) or plant on ridges 30â40 cm high. Ridges also warm the soil earlier in the season, which sweet potatoes like.

Slope matters for erosion. On slopes above 8%, plant across the slope (contour) and use vetiver grass or other barriers to slow runoff. In steep areas, terracing works but is labor-intensive. For most smallholders, a gentle slope with contour ridges is sufficient. Avoid steep slopes because heavy rain can wash away topsoil and expose roots.

Also consider aspect: in hot, dry regions, a north-facing slope (in southern hemisphere) or south-facing (northern hemisphere) gets less direct sun, reducing heat stress. In cooler highlands, a sunnier slope warms soil faster. Wind can also damage vines; plant windbreaks like napier grass or maize if strong winds are common.

Finally, check previous land use. Avoid fields that were recently in sweet potatoes or other root crops (carrots, cassava) due to shared pests like sweet potato weevil. Also, avoid fields with heavy weed pressure, especially couch grass. If you must use such a field, fallow it or plant a cover crop like mucuna for one season. A good field is one that drains well, has gentle slope, and hasn't had sweet potatoes for at least 2 years.

lessons.title: Land Clearing and Primary Tillage
lessons.body:
Start by clearing the field. Remove bushes, trees, and rocks. For small plots, use a machete or slasher. For larger areas, a brush cutter or tractor-mounted slasher saves time. Cut vegetation close to the ground and remove it or burn it (but burning loses nutrients; better to compost or use as mulch). If there are perennial weeds like couch grass or spear grass, dig out the roots â they will regrow if left. In Africa, many farmers use hand hoes (jembe) for clearing; it's labor-intensive but effective for small plots.

Primary tillage breaks up compacted soil and buries weeds. The goal is to loosen soil to 20â30 cm depth. You can use a hand hoe, ox-drawn plough, or tractor plough. For hand tillage, dig with a jembe, turning soil over. Do this when soil is moist but not wet â if it sticks to your tool, it's too wet. Tillage is best done at the start of the rains, so you can plant soon after. In dry areas, till after the first rains to avoid hard clods.

If using an ox-plough, plough to 15â20 cm depth. A tractor disc plough can go deeper (25â30 cm). Avoid ploughing too deep if subsoil is poor â you might bring up infertile clay. After ploughing, let the soil rest for a week or two to allow weeds to germinate, then do secondary tillage to kill them. This is called stale seedbed technique.

For no-till or minimum tillage, you can plant sweet potatoes into undisturbed soil if it's loose and well-drained. But most African soils benefit from some tillage to break hardpans. A hardpan is a compacted layer 15â20 cm down; test with a metal rod â if it won't penetrate, you need to break it. Use a chisel plough or hand hoe to fracture it.

Remember, primary tillage should be done once. Over-tilling destroys soil structure and organic matter. After tillage, the field is ready for secondary tillage and bed formation.

lessons.title: Secondary Tillage and Bed Formation
lessons.body:
Secondary tillage refines the seedbed. After primary ploughing, use a hand hoe or harrow to break clods and level the soil. The goal is a fine tilth â soil particles like breadcrumbs â so sweet potato roots can expand easily. Do this when soil is dry enough to crumble. If you're using a tractor, a disc harrow works well. For hand tools, a rake or hoe is fine. Remove any remaining weeds and rocks.

Sweet potatoes are usually grown on ridges or mounds. Ridges are long, raised beds; mounds are circular hills. Ridges are better for drainage and mechanization. Make ridges 30â40 cm high and 60â80 cm apart. For mounds, make them 30 cm high and 60 cm wide. The spacing depends on your variety and soil fertility. On poor soil, closer spacing (60 cm) gives more plants per hectare; on fertile soil, wider (80â100 cm) allows bigger roots.

To form ridges, use a hand hoe or ox-drawn ridger. Start by marking lines with a string. Then pull soil from both sides to form a ridge. In dry areas, make ridges flat-topped to conserve moisture; in wet areas, make them peaked to shed water. If you have a tractor, a ridger attachment makes quick work. For small plots, a hoe is fine â it takes about 2â3 days to ridge 1 hectare by hand.

Ridges should run across the slope (contour) to reduce erosion. If the field is flat, run them north-south for even sun exposure. Add compost or manure into the ridge before planting â mix it into the top 15 cm. This concentrates nutrients where roots will grow. You can also add a handful of wood ash per ridge for potassium.

After forming ridges, let them settle for a few days before planting. If it rains heavily, ridges may slump; repair them. A well-formed ridge warms up faster, drains excess water, and gives roots room to swell. This is critical for a good harvest.

lessons.title: Soil Amendments: Organic Matter and Compost
lessons.body:
Sweet potatoes respond well to organic matter. It improves soil structure, holds water, and feeds beneficial microbes. The best amendment is compost â decomposed plant and animal waste. Make compost by layering green materials (kitchen scraps, grass clippings) with brown materials (dry leaves, straw) and a little manure. Turn it every 2 weeks. In 2â3 months, you get dark, crumbly compost. Apply 5â10 tons per hectare (about 1â2 kg per square meter) before planting. Mix it into the top 15 cm of soil.

If you don't have compost, use well-rotted manure. Cow, goat, or poultry manure works, but poultry is high in nitrogen â use sparingly (2â3 tons/ha) to avoid excessive vines. Fresh manure can burn roots; let it age for at least 3 months. In Africa, many farmers keep livestock; collect manure and store it under cover to prevent nutrient loss from rain and sun.

Green manures are another option. Plant legumes like mucuna, lablab, or cowpeas in the off-season, then plough them under before they set seed. They add nitrogen and organic matter. For example, mucuna can produce 100â150 kg of nitrogen per hectare. This is a cheap way to fertilize. Also, crop residues like maize stalks can be chopped and incorporated, but they take longer to decompose.

Wood ash is a good source of potassium and raises pH. Apply 1â2 handfuls per ridge (about 500 kg/ha). But don't overdo it â too much ash can make soil too alkaline. If you have access to bone meal, it adds phosphorus. Rock phosphate is slow-release but effective in acidic soils.

Remember, organic matter is not a quick fix. It builds soil health over seasons. Start with whatever you have â even a small amount helps. Apply amendments 2â4 weeks before planting so they can integrate. Avoid applying fresh manure just before harvest, as it can introduce pathogens. Healthy soil grows healthy sweet potatoes.

lessons.title: Testing Soil and Interpreting Results
lessons.body:
Soil testing takes the guesswork out of farming. You can use a simple DIY kit or send samples to a lab. For a DIY kit, buy from an agro-dealer (cost $10â$20). It tests pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. To take a sample, collect soil from 10â15 spots across the field, digging 15 cm deep. Mix them in a clean bucket, then take a subsample of about 500g. Air-dry it, then follow kit instructions. For lab testing, contact your district agricultural office â many offer low-cost or free tests.

Interpret pH first. Sweet potatoes prefer 5.8â6.2. If pH is below 5.0, add lime (2â4 tons/ha) or wood ash. If above 7.0, add elemental sulfur or organic matter like pine needles. Lime takes 2â3 months to act, so apply before the season. For nitrogen, a reading of 0.1â0.2% is adequate. If low, add compost or a nitrogen fertilizer like urea (100 kg/ha). But too much nitrogen gives leafy vines and small roots.

Phosphorus should be 10â20 ppm (parts per million). If low, add bone meal or triple superphosphate (100 kg/ha). Potassium should be 100â200 ppm. If low, add wood ash or potassium sulfate (50â100 kg/ha). Remember, these are general guidelines â your local extension officer can give specific rates for your area. In many African soils, phosphorus is the most limiting nutrient.

Also test for organic matter. A simple test: put a tablespoon of soil in a jar with water, shake, and let settle. Organic matter floats. If less than 2%, add compost. Earthworms are a good sign â if you see none, soil is degraded.

Keep records of your test results and amendments. Over time, you'll see what works. If you can't test, observe your plants: yellow leaves = nitrogen; purple = phosphorus; brown edges = potassium. But testing is more accurate. Use results to make a fertilizer plan. For example, if pH is 5.5 and phosphorus is low, apply lime and bone meal. Then plant. Healthy soil = high yields.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil texture for sweet potato farming?
quiz.explanation: Sandy loam or loam provides good drainage and root expansion.

quiz.q: What is the preferred soil pH range for sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potatoes grow best in slightly acidic soil with pH 5.8â6.2.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes purple leaves in sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Purple leaves are a classic sign of phosphorus deficiency.

quiz.q: How much compost is recommended per hectare for sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Applying 5â10 tons of compost per hectare improves soil fertility and structure.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for drainage?
options: A) Dig a hole, fill with water, and see how long it takes to drain
B) Squeeze soil into a ball
C) Measure slope with a level
quiz.explanation: The water drainage test indicates how quickly excess water leaves the soil.

quiz.q: What slope is ideal for sweet potato fields?
quiz.explanation: A gentle slope of 2â5% allows drainage without causing erosion.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid low-lying areas for sweet potatoes?
options: B) They collect water and cause root rot
C) They have too many rocks
quiz.explanation: Waterlogged soil leads to root rot and poor yields.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of primary tillage?
options: B) To break up compacted soil and bury weeds
quiz.explanation: Primary tillage loosens soil and incorporates weeds to prepare for planting.

quiz.q: When is the best time to do primary tillage?
options: B) When soil is dry and hard
C) When soil is moist but not wet
quiz.explanation: Tilling moist soil is easier and avoids clod formation.

quiz.q: What is a hardpan?
options: B) A compacted soil layer that roots cannot penetrate
quiz.explanation: A hardpan is a dense layer that restricts root growth and drainage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for sweet potato ridges?
quiz.explanation: Ridges 30â40 cm high provide good drainage and root space.

quiz.q: Why should ridges run across the slope?
quiz.explanation: Contour ridges slow water runoff and prevent soil erosion.

quiz.q: What is the best material to add to ridges for potassium?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is rich in potassium and also raises soil pH.

quiz.q: How long does it take to make compost?
quiz.explanation: With regular turning, compost is ready in 2â3 months.

quiz.q: Which manure should be used sparingly due to high nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Poultry manure is high in nitrogen and can cause excessive vine growth.

quiz.q: What is a green manure?
options: B) A legume crop grown and ploughed under
quiz.explanation: Green manures are crops like mucuna that add nutrients when incorporated.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen can mucuna fix per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Mucuna is a powerful nitrogen fixer, adding 100â150 kg N per hectare.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of wood ash application per ridge?
quiz.explanation: 1â2 handfuls per ridge provides potassium without over-alkalizing soil.

quiz.q: How deep should you collect soil samples for testing?
quiz.explanation: Most soil tests require samples from the top 15 cm where roots feed.

quiz.q: What does a soil pH of 4.5 indicate?
quiz.explanation: pH 4.5 is strongly acidic and may require lime for sweet potatoes.

quiz.q: What is the ideal phosphorus level for sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: 10â20 ppm phosphorus is adequate for sweet potato growth.

quiz.q: Which amendment raises soil pH?
quiz.explanation: Lime is a common amendment to raise pH in acidic soils.

quiz.q: What does a jar test with soil and water show?
quiz.explanation: Organic matter floats, so the jar test estimates its percentage.

quiz.q: What is a sign of nitrogen deficiency in sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen deficiency causes pale, yellowish leaves.

quiz.q: How long before planting should you apply lime?
quiz.explanation: Lime needs 2â3 months to react and change soil pH.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for sweet potato ridges?
quiz.explanation: Ridges 60â80 cm apart allow good root development and airflow.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation important for sweet potatoes?
options: B) To prevent pest and disease buildup
quiz.explanation: Rotating with non-root crops breaks pest cycles like sweet potato weevil.

quiz.q: What is the first step in land clearing?
quiz.explanation: Clearing vegetation and obstacles is the initial step before tillage.

quiz.q: What tool is commonly used for primary tillage by smallholders in Africa?
quiz.explanation: The hand hoe is the most common tool for small-scale tillage in Africa.

quiz.q: What is the stale seedbed technique?
options: B) Letting weeds germinate then killing them before planting
C) Leaving soil fallow for a year
quiz.explanation: Stale seedbed reduces weed pressure by germinating and destroying weeds before crop planting.
